goals: Classify haloalkanes and name mono-, di- and tri-halo derivatives by common and IUPAC systems

slides.heading: Haloalkanes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — alkanes in which halogen atoms replace hydrogen: names, bonds, preparation and physical properties.

visual.alt: Table of familiar haloalkanes and their uses

slides.narration: Namaste! A cold spray on a footballer’s injured ankle, an anaesthetic in an operating theatre and an old refrigerator coolant all contain carbon bonded to a halogen. When halogen atoms replace hydrogen atoms in an alkane, we get a haloalkane. In this part we name and classify them, look at the carbon–halogen bond, learn several ways to make them, and explain their physical properties.

slides.heading: Classification
slides.body_md: By the **number of halogen atoms**: mono-, di- (**geminal**: both on one C; **vicinal**: on adjacent C), tri- and poly-halo compounds. Monohaloalkanes ($\ce{C_nH_{2n+1}X}$) are classified by the carbon bearing X.

rows: sp³ C next to a benzene ring

visual.alt: Table classifying haloalkanes

slides.narration: Haloalkanes with one halogen have the general formula C n H two n plus one X. We call them primary, secondary or tertiary according to how many carbons are attached to the carbon carrying the halogen. Allylic and benzylic halides have the halogen next to a double bond or a ring. Dihalides are geminal when both halogens are on the same carbon and vicinal when they are on neighbouring carbons.

slides.heading: Common and IUPAC names
slides.body_md: IUPAC: halogen as a **prefix** (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo) with a locant on the longest chain; prefixes in alphabetical order. Common names: alkyl group + halide.

visual.alt: Table of common and IUPAC names of haloalkanes

slides.narration: In IUPAC names the halogen is written as a prefix with a number for its position: one-bromopropane, two-bromo-two-methylpropane. Common names use the name of the alkyl group followed by halide, such as isobutyl chloride. Several polyhalogen compounds keep well-known common names: methylene chloride, chloroform and iodoform are dichloromethane, trichloromethane and triiodomethane.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming and classifying
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give IUPAC names and classify: (a) $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2Br}$; (b) $\ce{(CH3)3CCH2Cl}$; (c) $\ce{CH3CH2C(CH3)2I}$; (d) $\ce{CH2ClCH2Cl}$.

**(a)** 1-Bromo-2-methylpropane — primary (the CH₂Br carbon has one C neighbour).

**(b)** 1-Chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane — primary, although crowded.

**(c)** 2-Iodo-2-methylbutane — tertiary.

**(d)** 1,2-Dichloroethane — vicinal dihalide.

visual.alt: Flow for naming and classifying a haloalkane

slides.narration: Find the longest chain, number it for the lowest locants, and list prefixes alphabetically. Then look at the carbon carrying the halogen. In the first two examples that carbon has only one carbon neighbour, so both are primary, even though the second is very crowded. In the third, the carbon carrying iodine has three carbon neighbours, so it is tertiary. The last is a vicinal dichloride.

slides.heading: The carbon–halogen bond
slides.body_md: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is **polar**: carbon carries δ+ and is attacked by **nucleophiles**. Carbon is sp³ hybridised.

slides.narration: The halogen pulls the shared pair of electrons towards itself, leaving carbon with a small positive charge and the halogen with a small negative charge. Electron-rich nucleophiles are attracted to that positive carbon. This single fact explains why nucleophilic substitution is the typical reaction of haloalkanes, as we shall see in Part 2.

slides.heading: Bond length and bond enthalpy
slides.body_md: From F to I the halogen gets larger, so the C–X bond becomes **longer and weaker**; C–I breaks most easily, so iodoalkanes are the most reactive.

visual.alt: Table of carbon–halogen bond lengths and bond enthalpies

slides.narration: Down the halogen group the bond gets longer and much weaker, from about four hundred and fifty kilojoules per mole for carbon–fluorine to about two hundred and thirty for carbon–iodine. So for the same alkyl group, the order of reactivity is iodide, then bromide, then chloride, with fluorides the least reactive.

slides.heading: Preparation from alcohols
slides.body_md: The –OH group is replaced by a halogen. **Thionyl chloride** is preferred: its by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases, leaving pure haloalkane.

rows: Needed for 1° and 2°; 3° react with conc. HCl alone
HBr; HI (from NaBr or KI + acid)
Reactivity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl
PCl₃, PCl₅, PBr₃, PI₃ (red P + X₂)

visual.alt: Table of reagents for converting alcohols into haloalkanes

slides.narration: Alcohols are the usual starting point. Hydrogen chloride needs anhydrous zinc chloride to react with primary and secondary alcohols. Phosphorus halides give good yields; phosphorus tribromide and triiodide are made on the spot from red phosphorus and the halogen. Thionyl chloride is best, because sulphur dioxide and hydrogen chloride escape as gases, leaving the chloroalkane almost pure.

slides.heading: Preparation from alkanes and alkenes
slides.body_md: **Alkanes:** free-radical halogenation in light gives mixtures of isomers. **Alkenes:** add HX by **Markovnikov’s rule**; with HBr and a **peroxide**, anti-Markovnikov addition (Kharasch effect); X₂ gives vic-dihalides.

visual.alt: Table of preparations from alkanes and alkenes

slides.narration: Chlorinating an alkane in light gives a mixture of products, so it is rarely used for pure compounds. Adding hydrogen bromide to an alkene follows Markovnikov’s rule, putting bromine on the carbon with fewer hydrogens. But with a peroxide present, the addition is reversed and bromine goes to the end carbon. Adding bromine itself gives a vicinal dibromide.

slides.heading: Halide exchange and the Hunsdiecker reaction
slides.body_md: **Finkelstein:** R–Cl or R–Br + NaI in dry acetone → R–I; NaCl/NaBr precipitate, driving the reaction. **Swarts:** R–Cl/R–Br + AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃ → R–F. **Hunsdiecker:** the silver salt of a fatty acid with Br₂ in CCl₄ gives an alkyl bromide with **one carbon fewer**.

visual.alt: Table of halide exchange and the Hunsdiecker reaction

slides.narration: Iodo and fluoro compounds are made by swapping halogens. In the Finkelstein reaction, sodium iodide in dry acetone replaces chlorine or bromine, because the sodium chloride or bromide formed is insoluble in acetone and precipitates. In the Swarts reaction, metal fluorides give fluoroalkanes. In the Hunsdiecker reaction, the silver salt of a carboxylic acid is heated with bromine, losing carbon dioxide to give a bromoalkane with one carbon fewer.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing a preparation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Suggest a method: (a) butan-1-ol → pure 1-chlorobutane; (b) but-1-ene → 1-bromobutane; (c) 1-chlorobutane → 1-iodobutane; (d) silver butanoate → a bromoalkane (name it); (e) bromomethane → fluoromethane.

**(a)** SOCl₂ (gaseous by-products). **(b)** HBr with a peroxide. **(c)** NaI in dry acetone (Finkelstein).

**(d)** Br₂ in CCl₄, heat (Hunsdiecker): $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COOAg + Br2 -> CH3CH2CH2Br + CO2 + AgBr}$ — **1-bromopropane**.

**(e)** AgF (Swarts).

visual.alt: Table of conversions and methods

slides.narration: Match the method to the job. Thionyl chloride gives a pure chloroalkane from an alcohol. Hydrogen bromide with peroxide puts bromine on the end carbon of but-1-ene. Sodium iodide in acetone swaps chlorine for iodine. The Hunsdiecker reaction turns silver butanoate, with four carbons, into one-bromopropane, with three. And silver fluoride gives fluoromethane.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Lower members (CH₃Cl, CH₃Br, C₂H₅Cl) are gases; higher members are liquids or solids. Haloalkanes are **polar** and heavier than alkanes of similar size, so boiling points are higher. B.p. **rises** with chain length and halogen size (RI > RBr > RCl > RF) and **falls** with branching. Only slightly soluble in water (cannot form strong hydrogen bonds with water); soluble in organic solvents. RBr, RI and polychloro compounds are denser than water.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points of halomethanes

slides.narration: Haloalkanes boil higher than alkanes of similar size because their molecules are polar and heavier. The boiling point rises with chain length and with the size of the halogen, and falls with branching. Notice how adding more chlorine atoms to methane raises the boiling point step by step. Haloalkanes dissolve only slightly in water, because the attractions they form with water cannot repay the hydrogen bonds broken.

slides.heading: Worked example: boiling points of isomers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange the $\ce{C5H11Cl}$ isomers 1-chloropentane, 2-chloropentane and 2-chloro-2-methylbutane in order of increasing boiling point.

**Step 1.** Same molar mass, so compare shape.

**Step 2.** More branching → more compact molecules → smaller contact area → weaker van der Waals forces.

**Step 3.** 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane (≈ 358 K) < 2-chloropentane (≈ 370 K) < 1-chloropentane (≈ 381 K).

visual.alt: Table of three chloropentane isomers with branching and boiling points

slides.narration: The three isomers have the same formula, so the difference comes from shape. The straight chain of one-chloropentane gives the biggest surface for molecules to touch, so its van der Waals forces are strongest and it boils highest. The branched two-chloro-two-methylbutane is compact, touches its neighbours least and boils lowest.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Classify by the carbon bearing X (1°, 2°, 3°, allylic, benzylic); gem and vic dihalides.
IUPAC: halogen prefix with locant; CHCl₃ trichloromethane, CHI₃ triiodomethane.
C–X polar (C δ+); bond longer and weaker from F to I.
From alcohols (HX/ZnCl₂, PX₃, PCl₅, SOCl₂ best); alkenes (Markovnikov; peroxide effect with HBr); Finkelstein, Swarts; Hunsdiecker (one C fewer).
B.p. rises with mass, falls with branching; slightly soluble in water.

visual.alt: Summary table of key preparations

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Haloalkanes are classified by the carbon bearing the halogen and named with halogen prefixes. The carbon–halogen bond is polar and weakens from fluorine to iodine. They are made from alcohols, alkenes and alkanes, by halide exchange and by the Hunsdiecker reaction. Their boiling points rise with mass and fall with branching.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Give conditions with every equation (ZnCl₂, dry acetone, peroxide, CCl₄, light).
State why SOCl₂ is preferred and why Finkelstein goes to completion.
In the Hunsdiecker reaction, count carbons: the product has one fewer.
Peroxide effect works only with HBr.

slides.heading: Reactions of haloalkanes
slides.body_md: Part 2 — substitution, elimination, reactions with metals, and some important polyhalogen compounds.

visual.alt: Flow of the reactions of haloalkanes

slides.narration: The polar carbon–halogen bond makes haloalkanes the workhorses of organic synthesis. A nucleophile can replace the halogen; a base can remove the halogen with a hydrogen to make an alkene; and metals can join chains together or form Grignard reagents. We finish with chloroform, iodoform and the freons that damaged the ozone layer.

slides.heading: Substitution by nucleophiles
slides.body_md: A nucleophile replaces the halide: $\ce{Nu- + R-X -> R-Nu + X-}$. **Ambident** nucleophiles (CN⁻, NO₂⁻) attack through C/O with ionic K salts but through N with covalent Ag salts.

visual.alt: Table of substitution products of haloalkanes with nucleophiles

slides.narration: Here is the toolkit. Aqueous hydroxide gives alcohols; ammonia and amines give amines; sodium iodide gives iodoalkanes. Cyanide and nitrite are ambident: ionic potassium salts attack through carbon or oxygen, giving nitriles and alkyl nitrites, while covalent silver salts attack through nitrogen, giving isocyanides and nitroalkanes. Silver salts of acids give esters, and lithium aluminium hydride replaces the halogen by hydrogen.

slides.heading: The SN2 mechanism
slides.body_md: One step: the nucleophile attacks from the side **opposite** the halogen as the C–X bond breaks. Rate $= k[\ce{RX}][\ce{Nu-}]$ (second order). Configuration **inverted**. Reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance).

visual.alt: Table of SN2 reactivity

slides.narration: In the S N two mechanism everything happens in one step. The nucleophile approaches the carbon from the back, directly opposite the leaving halogen, so both species take part and the rate depends on both concentrations. Bulky groups block the backside, so methyl and primary halides react fastest by this route and tertiary halides hardly at all.

slides.heading: SN2: backside attack and inversion
slides.body_md: In the transition state carbon is partly bonded to both nucleophile and leaving group, with the other three groups in a plane. As the halide leaves, the three groups flip over: **Walden inversion**.

visual.alt: SN2 reaction of hydroxide with bromomethane: backside attack, a transition state with the three hydrogens in one plane, and an inverted product with bromide leaving
visual.caption: Schematic; the inversion is like an umbrella turning inside out in the wind.

slides.narration: Follow the picture. Hydroxide approaches from the side away from bromine. At the transition state the oxygen to carbon bond is half formed and the carbon to bromine bond half broken, with the three hydrogens flat. Then bromide leaves and the three groups flip over, like an umbrella in the wind. At a chiral carbon, this inverts the configuration.

slides.heading: The SN1 mechanism
slides.body_md: Two steps: (1) slow ionisation to a **carbocation**; (2) fast attack by the nucleophile. Rate $= k[\ce{RX}]$ (first order). Favoured by **3°**, allylic and benzylic halides (stable carbocations) and **polar protic** solvents. Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X.

visual.alt: Flow of the SN1 mechanism

slides.narration: The S N one mechanism happens in two steps. First the carbon–halogen bond breaks on its own, giving a carbocation; this slow step sets the rate, which depends only on the haloalkane. Then the nucleophile joins the carbocation quickly. Tertiary carbocations are most stable, so tertiary halides react fastest this way, especially in water or alcohols that stabilise the ions.

slides.heading: SN1 versus SN2 and optical rotation
slides.body_md: A carbon with four different groups is **chiral**; its enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions (d/+ and l/−). A 50 : 50 mixture is **racemic** (no rotation).
columns:
**SN2**

- One step
- Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]
- CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°
- Complete **inversion**: an optically active reactant gives an optically active product of opposite configuration

**SN1**

- Two steps via a planar carbocation
- Rate = k[RX]
- 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X
- **Racemisation** (attack on both faces): optical activity largely lost

visual.alt: Table comparing SN1 and SN2

slides.narration: Compare the two mechanisms. S N two is one step, second order, fastest for primary halides, and inverts a chiral carbon, so an optically active reactant gives an optically active product of opposite configuration. S N one goes through a flat carbocation, is first order and fastest for tertiary halides; the nucleophile can attack either face, so the product is largely racemic and optical activity is lost.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting rates
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Which reacts faster? (a) SN2 with $\ce{OH-}$: 1-chlorobutane or 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. (b) SN1 in water: 2-chloropropane or 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. (c) SN2 with $\ce{CN-}$: 1-bromopentane or 1-iodopentane.

**(a)** 1-Chlorobutane — primary, unhindered backside.

**(b)** 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane — tertiary carbocation is more stable.

**(c)** 1-Iodopentane — the C–I bond is weaker, so I⁻ is the better leaving group.

visual.alt: Table of three rate comparisons

slides.narration: First decide which mechanism is asked. For S N two, crowding matters, so the primary chloride wins. For S N one, carbocation stability matters, so the tertiary chloride wins. With the same alkyl group, the leaving group matters: the carbon–iodine bond is the weakest, so the iodide reacts faster than the bromide.

slides.heading: Quick check: SN1 or SN2
slides.body_md: Identify the mechanism from rate or stereochemical data.
slides.narration: Quick check. Does the rate depend on the nucleophile, and is the configuration inverted or racemised?

slides.heading: Worked example: one haloalkane, many products
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the product when 1-bromopropane reacts with (a) KCN, (b) AgCN, (c) KNO₂, (d) AgNO₂, (e) $\ce{CH3COOAg}$, (f) LiAlH₄.

**(a)** $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CN}$, butanenitrile. **(b)** $\ce{CH3CH2CH2NC}$, 1-isocyanopropane.

**(c)** $\ce{CH3CH2CH2ONO}$, propyl nitrite. **(d)** $\ce{CH3CH2CH2NO2}$, 1-nitropropane.

**(e)** $\ce{CH3COOCH2CH2CH3}$, propyl ethanoate. **(f)** $\ce{CH3CH2CH3}$, propane.

visual.alt: Table of products from 1-bromopropane

slides.narration: With potassium cyanide, the free cyanide ion attacks through carbon and the chain grows by one carbon to give butanenitrile. Silver cyanide is covalent, so only the nitrogen lone pair is free and an isocyanide forms. In the same way, potassium nitrite gives propyl nitrite while silver nitrite gives one-nitropropane. Silver ethanoate gives an ester, and lithium aluminium hydride gives propane.

slides.heading: Quick check: nucleophiles
slides.body_md: Predict the product of a haloalkane with a given nucleophile.
slides.narration: Quick check. For cyanide and nitrite, decide whether the potassium or the silver salt is used.

slides.heading: β-Elimination and Saytzeff’s rule
slides.body_md: With **alcoholic KOH** and heat, H from a β-carbon and X are removed to give an alkene (dehydrohalogenation). **Saytzeff’s rule:** the **more substituted** (more alkylated) alkene is the major product.

visual.alt: Table of elimination products by Saytzeff’s rule

slides.narration: In alcoholic potassium hydroxide, hydroxide acts as a base. It removes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the one carrying the halogen, and the halide leaves, forming a double bond. When more than one alkene can form, the one with more alkyl groups on the double bond is the major product. Aqueous hydroxide favours substitution; alcoholic hydroxide and heat favour elimination, especially for tertiary halides.

slides.heading: Reactions with sodium and magnesium
slides.body_md: **Wurtz reaction:** two alkyl halides couple with Na in dry ether; best for symmetrical alkanes. **Grignard reagent:** R–X + Mg in dry ether → RMgX, a strong nucleophile and base destroyed by water and other proton sources.

visual.alt: Table of reactions with sodium and magnesium

slides.narration: Sodium in dry ether joins two alkyl groups: the Wurtz reaction, which doubles the chain and works best when both halides are the same. Magnesium in dry ether gives a Grignard reagent, in which carbon is bonded to magnesium and behaves like a carbanion. Grignard reagents are very useful for building carbon chains but are destroyed by even traces of water, which give the alkane.

slides.heading: Quick check: elimination and metals
slides.body_md: Predict the alkene from an elimination, or the product of a Wurtz or Grignard reaction.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use Saytzeff’s rule for eliminations, and count carbons for the Wurtz reaction.

slides.heading: Chloroform (trichloromethane)
slides.body_md: **Preparation:** ethanol or acetone with bleaching powder (Cl₂ + Ca(OH)₂): chlorination then alkaline cleavage. **Properties:** colourless, sweet-smelling, heavy liquid (b.p. 334 K); slowly oxidised by air in light to poisonous **phosgene**, so stored in **dark, completely filled** bottles (a little ethanol added). Boiled with KOH it gives potassium methanoate; with conc. HNO₃ it gives chloropicrin; with silver powder, ethyne.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of chloroform

slides.narration: Chloroform is made by warming acetone or ethanol with bleaching powder: the methyl group is chlorinated and then split off by the alkali. It is a heavy, sweet-smelling liquid. In light, air slowly oxidises it to phosgene, a deadly gas, so it is stored in dark bottles filled to the brim with a little ethanol added. With nitric acid it gives chloropicrin, and with primary amines and alkali, the foul-smelling isocyanides of the carbylamine test.

slides.heading: Iodoform (triiodomethane)
slides.body_md: **Preparation:** ethanol or acetone warmed with iodine and NaOH (or Na₂CO₃): a **yellow crystalline precipitate** with a characteristic smell. **Iodoform test:** given by compounds containing **CH₃CO–** or **CH₃CH(OH)–** (ethanol, ethanal, propan-2-ol, acetone) but not by methanol or propan-1-ol. **Use:** antiseptic (liberates iodine).

visual.alt: Table of compounds and the iodoform test

slides.narration: Warm ethanol or acetone with iodine and sodium hydroxide, and yellow crystals of iodoform appear, with a distinctive medicinal smell. This is the iodoform test, given by compounds with a methyl group next to a carbonyl group, or next to a carbon carrying a hydroxyl group that can be oxidised to one. Ethanol and propan-2-ol give it; methanol and propan-1-ol do not. Iodoform was used as an antiseptic because it releases iodine.

slides.heading: Dichloromethane, tetrachloromethane and freons
slides.body_md: Useful polyhalogen compounds carry health and environmental costs.

rows: Harms the central nervous system; irritant
Formerly solvent and in making freons
Liver damage; reaches stratosphere and depletes ozone
Stable; in the stratosphere UV releases Cl• which destroys ozone

visual.alt: Table of dichloromethane, tetrachloromethane and freons

slides.narration: Dichloromethane is a good solvent and paint remover, but high exposure affects the nervous system. Tetrachloromethane, once a common solvent, damages the liver and helps destroy ozone. Freons, such as dichlorodifluoromethane, were ideal refrigerants because they are unreactive and non-toxic. That very stability lets them drift into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light releases chlorine atoms, each of which can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.

slides.heading: Quick check: polyhalogen compounds
slides.body_md: Identify a property, test or environmental effect of a polyhalogen compound.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the iodoform test and why chloroform and freons need care.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Nucleophiles: OH⁻ → ROH; NH₃ → RNH₂; KCN → RCN; AgCN → RNC; KNO₂ → RONO; AgNO₂ → RNO₂; R′COOAg → ester; LiAlH₄ → RH.
SN2: one step, second order, inversion, CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°. SN1: carbocation, first order, racemisation, 3° > 2° > 1°.
Alcoholic KOH: β-elimination; Saytzeff: more substituted alkene major.
Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na → R–R; Grignard: RX + Mg → RMgX (dry ether).
CHCl₃ → phosgene in light (dark full bottles); CHI₃ test for CH₃CO–/CH₃CH(OH)–; CFCs destroy ozone.

visual.alt: Summary table of SN1 and SN2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Nucleophiles replace the halogen by S N two, in one step with inversion, or by S N one, through a carbocation with racemisation. Alcoholic potassium hydroxide causes elimination following Saytzeff’s rule. Sodium couples haloalkanes and magnesium forms Grignard reagents. Chloroform, iodoform, dichloromethane, tetrachloromethane and freons each have uses, and some serious hazards.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Specify aqueous KOH (substitution) or alcoholic KOH (elimination).
Give rate law and stereochemistry for each mechanism.
K salts: attack via C (CN⁻) or O (NO₂⁻); Ag salts: via N.
Mention phosgene and dark, full bottles for chloroform storage.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Always state aqueous or alcoholic potassium hydroxide. For mechanisms, give the rate law and the stereochemistry. Learn which salts attack through which atom. And for chloroform, mention phosgene and how the bottles are filled and stored.

sections.heading: 1. Classification, names and the C–X bond
sections.body_md:
Monohaloalkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X: **1°, 2°, 3°** by the carbon bearing X; allylic and benzylic halides; **gem** (both X on one C) and **vic** (adjacent C) dihalides; tri- and polyhalides. IUPAC: halogen prefix + locant (2-bromo-2-methylpropane); CH₂Cl₂ dichloromethane, CHCl₃ trichloromethane (chloroform), CHI₃ triiodomethane (iodoform).

C–X is **polar** (C δ+), attacked by nucleophiles. Bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases F → I (C–Cl 351, C–Br 293, C–I 234 kJ mol⁻¹), so reactivity RI > RBr > RCl.

Halogen atoms on adjacent carbons, e.g. CH₂BrCH₂Br.

sections.heading: 2. Preparation
sections.body_md:
- **Alkanes:** X₂, light (free radical; mixtures).
- **Alkenes:** HX (Markovnikov); HBr + peroxide (anti-Markovnikov); X₂ → vic-dihalide.
- **Alcohols:** HCl/ZnCl₂ (Lucas), HBr, HI; PCl₃, PCl₅, PBr₃ (red P + Br₂); **SOCl₂ best** (SO₂, HCl gases).
- **Finkelstein:** RCl/RBr + NaI, dry acetone → RI (NaCl/NaBr precipitate).
- **Swarts:** RCl/RBr + AgF, Hg₂F₂, SbF₃ → RF.
- **Hunsdiecker:** RCOOAg + Br₂ (CCl₄, heat) → RBr + CO₂ + AgBr (one C fewer).

key_terms.definition_md: Exchange of Cl or Br for I using NaI in dry acetone.
Silver salt of a carboxylic acid + Br₂ → bromoalkane with one carbon fewer.

sections.heading: 3. Physical properties
sections.body_md: CH₃Cl, CH₃Br, C₂H₅Cl are gases; higher members liquids/solids. B.p. higher than alkanes of similar size (polar, heavier); rises with chain length and halogen size (RI > RBr > RCl > RF); falls with branching (smaller surface area). Slightly soluble in water (cannot repay water’s H-bonds), soluble in organic solvents. RBr, RI, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ denser than water.

key_terms.definition_md: Weak intermolecular attractions that increase with molecular size and contact area.

sections.heading: 4. Nucleophilic substitution: SN1 and SN2
sections.body_md:
**SN2:** one step, backside attack; rate $= k[\ce{RX}][\ce{Nu-}]$; **inversion** (Walden); CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°.
**SN1:** slow ionisation to a planar carbocation, then fast attack; rate $= k[\ce{RX}]$; **racemisation**; 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X; favoured by polar protic solvents; benzylic/allylic fast.

**Optical activity:** a chiral carbon (four different groups) gives enantiomers that rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions (d/+, l/−); racemic mixture inactive.

key_terms.definition_md: Inversion of configuration at carbon in an SN2 reaction.
Equal amounts of two enantiomers; optically inactive.

sections.heading: 6. Elimination and reactions with metals
sections.body_md:
**β-Elimination:** alcoholic KOH, heat → alkene; **Saytzeff:** more substituted alkene is major (2-bromopentane → pent-2-ene). Aqueous KOH → substitution; alcoholic KOH → elimination (especially 3°).

**Wurtz:** $\ce{2RX + 2Na ->[dry ether] R-R + 2NaX}$ (symmetrical alkanes). **Grignard:** $\ce{RX + Mg ->[dry ether] RMgX}$; $\ce{RMgX + H2O -> RH + Mg(OH)X}$.

key_terms.definition_md: In dehydrohalogenation the more substituted alkene is the major product.
An alkylmagnesium halide, RMgX, made from RX and Mg in dry ether.

sections.heading: 7. Polyhalogen compounds
sections.body_md:
**Chloroform:** from ethanol or acetone + bleaching powder; oxidised in light to **phosgene** ($\ce{2CHCl3 + O2 -> 2COCl2 + 2HCl}$) — stored in dark, full bottles with a little ethanol; with conc. HNO₃ → chloropicrin CCl₃NO₂; with KOH → HCOOK; with Ag → C₂H₂; carbylamine test with 1° amines.
**Iodoform:** ethanol/acetone + I₂ + NaOH → yellow CHI₃; test for CH₃CO– and CH₃CH(OH)–; antiseptic.
**CH₂Cl₂:** solvent, paint remover; affects the nervous system. **CCl₄:** non-polar (tetrahedral); liver damage; ozone depletion. **Freons (CFCs, e.g. CCl₂F₂):** refrigerants; UV in stratosphere releases Cl• which destroys O₃.

key_terms.definition_md: COCl₂, a poisonous gas formed by oxidation of chloroform in light.
Yellow CHI₃ with I₂/NaOH, given by CH₃CO– and CH₃CH(OH)– compounds.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- KCN → isocyanide (wrong: it gives a nitrile; AgCN gives isocyanide).
- SN1 gives inversion (wrong: racemisation).
- Using the peroxide effect with HCl (only HBr).
- Forgetting that the Hunsdiecker product has one carbon fewer.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Mechanisms (2–3 marks): steps, rate law, stereochemistry.
- Products (1 mark each): correct structure and name.
- Polyhalogen compounds: equation plus a use or hazard.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of isopentyl bromide, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Br, is:

questions.stem_md: Among the halomethanes CH₃F, CH₃Cl, CH₃Br and CH₃I, which carbon–halogen bond is the longest and weakest?
questions.solution_md: Bond length rises and bond enthalpy falls from F to I (C–I about 214 pm, 234 kJ mol⁻¹) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? 3-Bromoprop-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂Br, is a vinylic halide.

questions.stem_md: For the SN2 reaction of 1-bromopropane with hydroxide ions, the initial rate is $2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ when $[\text{RBr}] = [\ce{OH-}] = 0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. Calculate the rate constant in L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Rate $= k[\text{RBr}][\ce{OH-}]$, so $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \div (0.10 \times 0.10) = 0.020\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: The reaction of hydroxide ions with 1-chlorobutane is second order, but 2-chloro-2-methylpropane hardly reacts by this route. Explain both observations.

answer.model_answer_md: With 1-chlorobutane the reaction is SN2: one step in which OH⁻ attacks the carbon from the back as Cl⁻ leaves, so both species are in the rate-determining step: rate = k[RCl][OH⁻]. In 2-chloro-2-methylpropane the three methyl groups block backside approach (steric hindrance), so SN2 is very slow; it reacts instead by SN1.

questions.solution_md: One step, both species; steric hindrance.

questions.stem_md: Describe the SN1 mechanism for the hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in aqueous acetone. Give the rate law and explain why tertiary halides favour this mechanism.

answer.model_answer_md: Step 1 (slow): $\ce{(CH3)3CBr -> (CH3)3C+ + Br-}$, forming a planar tertiary carbocation. Step 2 (fast): $\ce{(CH3)3C+ + H2O -> (CH3)3COH + H+}$ (or OH⁻ attack). Rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr], first order. Three alkyl groups stabilise the carbocation by their +I effect (and hyperconjugation) and hinder backside attack, so SN1 is favoured.

questions.solution_md: Two steps; rate = k[RBr]; stable 3° carbocation.

questions.stem_md: Compare the stereochemical outcome when (a) optically active 2-bromooctane reacts with concentrated NaOH in acetone by SN2 and (b) optically active 3-chloro-3-methylheptane is hydrolysed in water by SN1. Explain each.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the SN1 mechanism for the hydrolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, giving the rate law. [2]

(b) What is the stereochemical outcome when an optically active secondary bromide reacts by SN2? Explain. [1½]

(c) Arrange CH₃Br, CH₃CH₂Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr and (CH₃)₃CBr in order of increasing reactivity (i) by SN1 and (ii) by SN2. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Step 1 (slow): $\ce{(CH3)3CCl -> (CH3)3C+ + Cl-}$. Step 2 (fast): $\ce{(CH3)3C+ + OH- -> (CH3)3COH}$. Rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl] (first order).

(b) Inversion of configuration (Walden inversion): the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving bromide; in the transition state the three other groups lie in a plane and then flip over, so the product is optically active with the opposite configuration.

(c) (i) SN1: CH₃Br < CH₃CH₂Br < (CH₃)₂CHBr < (CH₃)₃CBr. (ii) SN2: (CH₃)₃CBr < (CH₃)₂CHBr < CH₃CH₂Br < CH₃Br.

questions.solution_md: Two-step SN1; inversion; opposite orders.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give the main organic product when chloroethane reacts with (i) KCN, (ii) AgCN, (iii) KNO₂, (iv) AgNO₂ and (v) LiAlH₄. [2½]

(b) Explain why KCN and AgCN give different products. [1½]

(c) Why is excess ammonia used to prepare ethanamine from chloroethane? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN. (ii) Ethyl isocyanide (isocyanoethane), CH₃CH₂NC. (iii) Ethyl nitrite, CH₃CH₂ONO. (iv) Nitroethane, CH₃CH₂NO₂. (v) Ethane.

(b) CN⁻ is ambident. KCN is ionic, so free CN⁻ attacks through the more nucleophilic carbon, giving a nitrile. AgCN is covalent (Ag–C bond), so only the nitrogen lone pair is available, giving an isocyanide.

(c) The ethanamine formed is itself a nucleophile and can react with more chloroethane to give secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary salt; a large excess of NH₃ makes reaction with NH₃ much more likely.

questions.solution_md: Five products; ambident CN⁻; excess NH₃ limits polyalkylation.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations for the preparation of chloroform from ethanol and bleaching powder, taking bleaching powder as a source of Cl₂ and Ca(OH)₂. [2]

(b) Write the equation for the iodoform reaction of ethanol and state two observations. [1½]

(c) What are freons? Explain, with equations, how they damage the ozone layer. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Ethanol is oxidised to ethanal, which is chlorinated and then cleaved: $\ce{CH3CH2OH + Cl2 -> CH3CHO + 2HCl}$; $\ce{CH3CHO + 3Cl2 -> CCl3CHO + 3HCl}$; $\ce{2CCl3CHO + Ca(OH)2 -> 2CHCl3 + (HCOO)2Ca}$.

(b) $\ce{C2H5OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH -> CHI3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H2O}$. Yellow crystalline precipitate; characteristic antiseptic smell.

(c) Freons are chlorofluorocarbons such as CCl₂F₂, once used as refrigerants and propellants. Being inert, they reach the stratosphere, where UV light breaks them: $\ce{CF2Cl2 ->[UV] CF2Cl + Cl}$; the Cl atoms destroy ozone catalytically: $\ce{Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2}$, $\ce{ClO + O -> Cl + O2}$.
